==Problem==
Consider all positive four-digit integers consisting of only even digits. What fraction of these integers are divisible by <imath>4</imath>?

<imath>\textbf{(A) }\frac{1}{4}\qquad\textbf{(B) }\frac{2}{5}\qquad\textbf{(C) }\frac{1}{2}\qquad\textbf{(D) }\frac{3}{5}\qquad\textbf{(E) }\frac{3}{4}</imath>

==Solution 1==
The divisibility rule for <imath>4</imath> is that the last 2 digits must be a multiple of <imath>4</imath>. Because of this, we can "discard" the first two digits, as the last two digits are the only ones that matter (this doesn't actually change the answer, since for every possible case that the first two digits can be, there are the same number of cases the last two digits can be, so the ratio of cases that work to the cases that don't work is still the same). We can also notice that the tens digit also doesn't matter, since every single digit in the number must be even. Therefore, we only need to care about the ones digit. We have the even digits <imath>0</imath>, <imath>2</imath>, <imath>4</imath>, <imath>6</imath>, and <imath>8</imath>, and there are 3 digits that are divisible by <imath>4</imath>, namely <imath>0</imath>, <imath>4</imath>, and <imath>8</imath>, out of <imath>5</imath> total digits, so we have the final fraction <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }\frac{3}{5}}</imath>. 
~Baihly2024

==Solution 2==

A number is divisible by 4 if and only if the last two digits are divisible by 4. Then, the third and fourth digits must be divisible by 4. So, those possibilities are <imath> \{(00), (04), (08), (12), (16), (20),\dots,(96)\} </imath>. There are 25 cases in this, however, some of these are odd! Luckily, each odd tens digit would have an even units digit of either 2 or 6 on the third or fourth multiples, meaning each sequence of 5 between 4 and 20 actually contributes 3 to the count, giving us <imath> 5(3) - 1 + 1 = 15 </imath> actual cases.

Then, the remaining two numbers are to be consisting of the digits <imath> \{0,2,4,6,8\} </imath>. The first digit has 4 choices, and the next has 5, giving a total of 20 unique combinations. These 20 combinations can go with any of the other 24 combinations, giving 300 total combinations. There are a total of <imath> 4 \times 5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125 \times 4 = 500 </imath> four digit integers whose digits are all even. The fraction is <imath> 300/500 = \boxed{3/5} </imath>

~Pinotation
